Short answer: it’s mostly an energy/size artifact plus co-exposure and measurement issues. In NHANES, people who eat more calories consume more of every nutrient (Na, K, Mg) and also tend to have higher diastolic BP via body size, alcohol, and overall dietary pattern. If you analyze absolute intakes without proper energy adjustment and co-nutrient control, all three minerals will look positively associated with DBP—even though potassium and magnesium lower BP in trials.

What’s driving the paradox
- Confounding by total energy and body size: Absolute Na/K/Mg intakes scale with calories. Higher energy intake correlates with larger body size/adiposity and higher BP. Without appropriate energy adjustment, you estimate “more food” rather than “more nutrient per unit energy.”
- Nutrient co-exposure: In typical US diets, Na, K, and Mg rise together with total food quantity. If you don’t adjust Na and K for each other (or use the Na:K ratio), potassium will partially proxy sodium, pushing its association with BP upward. Same for magnesium.
- Measurement error in diet recalls: Single-day (or even two-day) 24-hour recalls are noisy and systematically underreport sodium (especially in people with higher BMI). Non-differential error combined with confounding can attenuate or even flip signs when exposures are highly correlated with energy and each other.
- Reverse causation and treatment: People with hypertension are advised to change diet; many are on diuretics that lower K/Mg and may take supplements or alter intake. Medication use, diagnosis, and counseling can distort cross-sectional associations.
- Model specification issues: 
  - Not using survey design/weights can bias results.
  - Over- or under-adjusting (e.g., omitting alcohol; mis-specifying BMI/waist; not handling antihypertensive treatment) can leave residual confounding.
  - Multicollinearity among Na/K/Mg can make coefficients unstable if modeled together without care.

How to check
- Refit models using nutrient densities (mg per 1000 kcal) or the residual method for Na, K, Mg, with total energy in the model.
- Mutually adjust for sodium and potassium or use the Na:K ratio (often a stronger and more causal proxy).
- Average both recall days; adjust for weekday/weekend and exam vs interview day; consider the NCI usual intake method to reduce within-person error.
- Exclude implausible energy reporters; run stratified analyses by BMI category.
- Adjust for age, sex, race/ethnicity, height, BMI or waist, alcohol, smoking, physical activity, socioeconomic factors, diabetes/CKD, and antihypertensive medication (and consider adding a treatment constant to BP).
- Separate foods from supplements; do a sensitivity analysis excluding supplement users and those on potassium-sparing/loop diuretics.
- Inspect collinearity (VIFs) and consider focusing on Na:K rather than including highly collinear nutrients simultaneously.

What you’ll likely see after fixes
- Sodium (energy-adjusted) positively associated with DBP.
- Potassium (energy- and sodium-adjusted, or as lower Na:K) inversely associated with DBP.
- Magnesium (energy-adjusted, with K/overall diet quality accounted for) weakly inverse or null.
- Effects remain small per unit change, consistent with RCT magnitudes.

Bottom line: Cross-sectional NHANES associations using absolute intakes mostly reflect “how much people eat” and correlated dietary patterns, not the causal mineral effects seen in trials. Use energy-adjusted nutrients, consider Na:K, correct for measurement error, and carefully control confounding to align observational estimates with RCT evidence.
